creator: Alexander Terp
description:
Agents in Muster panes have no good way to talk to each other. The two tools built for it deliver through a keyboard or a poll, and neither reaches across machines. This card holds the design conversation of 2026-09-17 (Alex and Claude) about giving Muster a message daemon of its own, and the related question of how much of herdr should stay under it. Nothing here is a MIP yet. Each section says what leans which way and what is open.

## What is wrong today

`muster pane send` types into a pty. That is fine for a line and wrong for a message. A Return arriving mid-paste submits the fragment so far. A long paste folds into a `[Pasted text #N]` placeholder that waits for a human's Return. A pane at a dialog answers its first option to any Return. Exit 0 means the daemon took the text, not that the program received it (`docs/cli/limits.md`, a_2LOHfLmsL). A devenv pane cannot send at all (a_29e9be7aQ), the text can only come from the command line (a_2M9T8iOgk), and the only way to wait for another agent is to poll `window --json` (a_2M9T8O6dL).

The 1024-byte cap is the kernel's `MAX_CANON`: 1024 on macOS, 4095 on Linux. It applies only while the pane's program reads in canonical mode, and it discards the whole line rather than cutting it (`docs/observations/herdr-0.8.0.md` section 25). Harnesses read in raw mode, so it does not bind them. It is one more reason the keyboard is not a data channel, not a constraint on this design.

Council v1 (amterp/council, Go, last commit 2026-01-04) has the group semantics: a shared transcript, turn order, optimistic locking, a moderator view. Its transport is a JSONL file per session, polled every 2 s under a timeout, with agents tracking event numbers by hand, on one machine. Its board records agents stuck awaiting and agents leaving prematurely. Its code and its debt are not carried; v2 is re-derived below.

Claude Code 2.1.224+ can message between its own sessions on one machine (`ListAgents`, `SendMessage`), delivered between the receiver's tool calls or starting a turn if it is idle. Across machines it rides Remote Control, which an organization policy at work disables. It is also Claude-only.

## Direction, as it stands

Leaning, agreed in conversation and not yet argued in a MIP:

- Muster owns the code and the distribution. Attention routing is Muster's founding concern and an unread message is an attention event. `[[daemon]]` blocks already name the machines. The pinned-binary install to `~/.muster/bin` and the SSH master's socket forwarding (`muster-ssh`) are the deployment and the transport. `muster-proto` is already meant to be the agent-facing API (MIP-1). `pane send` is a messaging primitive Muster already owns, and this would supersede it.
- The daemon is a process built from this repo, one per machine, beside herdr. Not in the window, because quitting Muster must keep costing nothing. Today the only daemon Muster runs is herdr's binary under Muster's session; this would be the first of Muster's own.
- The dependency arrow points from Muster to the message daemon and never back. A headless agent in a plain terminal, never in a pane, must be able to join. Crate boundaries enforce it: a core with no Muster dependency, one crate per adapter, and Muster's core depending on a thin client for display.
- The core is workflow-free: participants, messages, addressing, and groups whose policy is data. Presets, manners, and what a council is convened for live in skills, not in Muster. That is how the no-imposed-workflow and no-special-casing-one-harness rules survive a feature that is workflow-shaped.
- Adapters carry everything harness- or backend-shaped: a wake adapter (deliver text to a participant), a presence source (alive, gone, busy, blocked), a store, a transport. Claude's inbox socket is one wake adapter. herdr is one presence source and one fallback wake adapter, typing a single short line into a pane. A pull adapter serves agents whose hooks drain their queue themselves. Same rule as for herdr and for Claude generally (a_2AJS0Xz7I): one thing we support, never the thing we are.

Open:

- Whether the agent-facing verbs are `muster` subcommands on both platforms, so agents learn one tool, or a separate binary. Either way the daemon and its CLI must build for Linux, which no Muster artifact does yet. A Linux `muster` that talks to the local daemon is also most of what a_29e9be7aQ lacks.
- Language. Rust follows from living in this repo and sharing `muster-ssh`, `muster-herdr`, `muster-proto`.
- Cross-machine shape. Proposed: a group or participant has a home daemon, the one where it was created; other daemons forward posts to it and replicate its log over the forwarded socket. One writer per log, remote posts fail loudly when the link is down, local pairs keep working offline.
- Whether visibility follows addressing. Proposed: addressing decides who is woken, never who may read; everything is in the log; no private messages in v2. Noise is wasted turns, not readable lines.
- What the daemon enforces and what prompting carries. Proposed: exactly two things enforced, who may address whom and which participants an unaddressed post wakes, because a rule a council is convened with has to hold on turn 40 when the prompt has faded. Everything else is skill text.
- How the human sees it: a badge on the sidebar row, a transcript in a pane, both, or a web view like council v1's.

## The model, re-derived

Five concepts came out of starting clean. Nothing else has earned a place yet.

- **Participant.** A name, a machine, and a wake address the daemon learned at join. Two agents side by side each `join`, `who`, and `post --to`, with no group and no convening. Gone when it leaves or its wake address dies.
- **Message.** From, to, body, sequence number. `to` names participants or a group. Every message lands in the shared log.
- **Group.** Optional. A named set with a policy: which members an unaddressed post wakes (its ring set) and an allow-matrix of who may address whom. A convened council is a group. A director is a participant the policy points at; the daemon has no concept of one.
- **Delivery.** The daemon computes who to wake, coalesces so a participant with unread content is woken once per batch, and hands each wake to an adapter. A read cursor per participant makes `read` mean "my unread", and lets `post` refuse when the poster has unread. That is council v1's stale-context guard without the agent counting events.
- **Adapter.** As above: wake, presence, store, transport.

## Facts established on 2026-09-17

- A Bash child of a Claude session can post into that session's inbox. Connect to `$CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET`, send `{"type":"auth","token":"$CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN"}` and then `{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":"..."}}`, one JSON object per line. Tested: the text arrived between tool calls as a peer message. The example is embedded in the Claude binary's own help text, and the docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging) describe scripts posting this way. The socket lives at `/run/user/<uid>/cc-socks/<pid>.sock` on Linux.
- Registration makes the wake address free: the agent runs `join` from inside its session, the CLI inherits the socket path, and hands it over. No pane-to-pid mapping and no herdr involved.
- Still to test: the docs say a non-child sender, which the daemon is, is delivered to a session in a prompting permission class (auto mode included) and held for approval by one that bypasses permissions. The receiver drops identical repeats arriving within a short window, so wake texts must differ per batch. About a million characters per message; around 50 queued.
- `claude remote-control --help` on the devenv: disabled by organization policy.

## How much is herdr buying us?

Raised by Alex as part of this story: keep herdr under Muster, or build exactly what Muster needs and own it. `docs/origin.md` "The decision" names three exit lanes, cheapest first: fork herdr, replace it wholesale with the contract corpus as the spec, or adapt another backend. a_26BJbJeZL records an unresolved disagreement about the first lane. This card puts the second on the table.

What herdr provides today: PTYs owned by a daemon that outlives clients. The tree and cwds surviving a daemon restart, though processes and scrollback do not (observations section 12). Agent state by server-side screen analysis, with no hooks and the same behavior local and remote. Server-rendered frame diffs to the surface. One socket protocol that is identical over SSH (section 8).

What Muster already does itself around it: encodes input blind with `muster-vt`'s key encoder, because `terminal.input` is a raw write and the modes are invisible (section 5). Derives `done` rather than reading it. Rebuilds the tree from rects and ignores herdr's geometry. Supervises reconnects and takeovers. Ships, pins, and installs the daemon on every machine.

What it costs: fifteen of the 23 cards in `uncommitted` are herdr findings or herdr decisions, among them one render thread for every attached pane with typing waiting behind it (a_2KHGXkKSc), a subscription per pane for agent state (a_27N6pklkl), a thousand rows of history and no search (a_29Ayr1P8F), and invisible input modes (a_27CTRluw7). Upstream is about 222k lines of Rust with weekly releases, and Muster holds one pin.

What an own daemon would have to provide: spawn and own PTYs; persist across client exit and define restart semantics; hold a headless terminal per pane, which `muster-vt` already wraps libghostty-vt for; stream frames; encode input where the modes live; detect agent state across harnesses; install and run remotely, which Muster already does for herdr's binary. Agent-state detection is the largest single thing herdr has and Muster has not, and the part to size before anything else.

Considerations, none settled. The corpus's authority: today it is recorded from herdr, so it is reality; recorded from a daemon we wrote, it is a spec we set ourselves (the reservation in a_26BJbJeZL). The fallback property in origin.md, that a rough Muster never blocks a workday because the herdr TUI still works against the same daemons, goes away with an own daemon. The message daemon is Muster's first daemon regardless, so a pane daemon later could be a second process or the same one; keeping them separate lets this question be decided on its own.

## Prior art looked at

hcom (aannoo/hcom): hooks record to SQLite and inject messages between tool calls; `@tag` groups; spawn, fork, kill; an MQTT relay for cross-machine, which the work policy above rules out. Its collision detection, telling two agents that edited the same file within 30 seconds, is worth borrowing later. Cyclops (cyclops-team/cyclops): a durable mailbox plus a one-line "doorbell" typed into a tmux pane, with a guard that waits while a human is mid-draft; single tmux server only. A2A is the enterprise service-agent protocol and not this problem.
title: 📨 Agents messaging each other: a daemon of Muster's own, and whether herdr stays under it
